definition: Restive means restless and impatient under restraint, straining against control or delay while still being held in check.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word restive. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know restive should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The colts grew restive in the starting gate as the third false start was announced.
Impatient is weaker than restive: an impatient person merely wants the wait to end, while a restive one is visibly beginning to strain against whatever is holding things up.
Mutinous is stronger than restive — a mutinous crowd is on the edge of open revolt, while a restive one is still contained, just barely and unhappily.

Fidgety means unable to stay still — tapping, shifting, checking the clock — restless energy with no particular target. Restive gives that energy a grievance: restless impatience straining against the specific restraint or delay causing it. A fidgety child squirms anywhere; a restive one squirms against the seatbelt.

Uneasy means unsettled and vaguely anxious, a discomfort that may have no clear cause at all. Restive is sharper and points outward: restless impatience straining against a known restraint or delay. An uneasy audience worries quietly; a restive one starts pushing at whatever holds it.

The documentary crew had promised the villagers a ten-minute ceremony before filming began.
An hour later, cables still snaked across the square and the director kept calling for one more lighting check.
Children broke from their parents to chase pigeons; two elders stood and stretched pointedly; a low murmur ran through the rows of folding chairs.
The longer the delay stretched, the more restive the crowd became — not angry yet, but visibly done with waiting.
The murmuring, pointed stretching, and children drifting off show a crowd growing restless and resistant under an imposed delay — the exact condition restive names.
formal; journalistic (crowds, legislatures, animals)

Restive describes impatience under restraint or delay — a held crowd, a waiting horse, a stalled legislature — which distinguishes it from this unit's combative: a restive group strains against being made to wait, while a combative one is actively spoiling for a fight or argument.

The storm pinned Halley Research Station shut for nine straight days, and the safety officer's rule was absolute: nobody stepped outside.
By the sixth day the crew had grown openly restive.
The delay itself was bearable; the order holding them indoors was what they strained against.
Two glaciologists demanded a waiver to check their instruments.
A cook was found half-suited in the airlock, arguing that the wind had dropped.
The station manager wrote in her log that the mood was not boredom.
It was pressure against a rule, rising a little with every hour the rule held.
When the wind finally eased on day nine, the door opened to a line of people already dressed, packed, and pushing to be first through it.
